title.en: How Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of a Sorcerer and His Seven Sisters
title.zh: 火雞童捏心記：巫師與其七姊妹之亡

region.en: Lonely lodge of the old grandmother, and the strawberry clearing to the east
region.zh: 老祖母的孤屋與東方草莓林間空地

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 23, 'Turkey Boy Squeezed the Hearts of Sorcerers' (1923)

summary.en: An old woman and her grandson Turkey live alone in an old lodge, all their people killed by the monster wizard Deadoehdjadse' who lives to the east near a bed of strawberries as large as hearts. In the forbidden room Turkey finds the drum and the lacrosse ball, and learns the secret from Skin Man, the dried human skin swinging on a pole: he borrows a mole's coat, burrows underground, buys the mysteries with wampum beads stained with berry juice, and learns that the lives of the sorcerer and his seven sisters are secure, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swims in a pool under a bed in the lodge. Made up to look exactly like Deadoehdjadse' and chewing a strawberry, he eats the human flesh his sisters set before him, then - when Skin Man cries that the deer are in the strawberries - lifts the bed, commands the loon, grabs the eight hearts and runs: 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.' Squeezing each heart as the sisters close with their deer-clubs, he fells them one by one and cracks every heart open on the flat killing-stone like flint. The Skin Man taunts the returning sorcerer - 'Turkey has your heart' - and his own heart breaks on the rock; patted all over, Skin Man is restored to his normal form: Turkey's own brother, held by sorcery. From the bones strewn on the flat rock they raise a host of quarreling people with mismatched limbs, pacify them, and with the grandmother's people build a new village by the strawberries, where they live to this day.
summary.zh: 老嫗與孫兒火雞相依為命，族人盡喪於東方巫魔迪多耶茲之手。禁室裡，火雞偷擊鼓、偷玩袋棍球，又借鼴鼠之皮鑽地而行，以染莓汁的貝珠向「皮人」購得奧秘：巫魔與七姊妹的心藏在屋中一張床下的水潭裡、由一隻潛鳥挾於翼下看守。火雞幻化成巫魔模樣，嚼著草莓吐汁，吞下姊妹們奉上的人肉；待皮人高呼「鹿進草莓地了」引開眾女，他掀床、令潛鳥、奪得八顆心臟奔出：「我是火雞，你們的心都在我手裡！」眾女持鹿棒追來，他便一顆顆捏心使其昏厥，再把心臟逐一摔在殺人石上，如燧石般迸裂。歸來的巫魔被皮人嘲弄——「火雞拿了你的心」——心石俱碎；皮人經他遍體拍撫復原，竟是受妖術所制的親哥哥。二人拾骨堆山，踢倒山核桃樹喊「散骨之眾，趁樹未倒快起！」——眾人肢體錯配、爭吵不休；火雞安撫之後，偕祖母一家在草莓地旁重建新村，安居至今。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cannibalism is the villain's own trait, narrated at story distance.

passages.text: The lodge was old and very large, but only the two lived in it, for all others had been killed by sorcerers. Winter was coming on and the old woman was busily engaged each day in gathering firewood for the winter's store. Every day she would cry as she started on her journey and when she returned she would cry again... 'All of our people are dead. They have been destroyed by a monster wizard who eats human flesh. His lodge is to the east and near it is a great bed of strawberries. Oh, they are as large as hearts. Once there was a good village of our tribe there, but the people were killed and the houses have now fallen down.' Turkey now said, 'My grandmother, now is the time for me to go... Make me some moccasins. I am going east.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 200-202; not verbatim.

passages.text: Turkey was cautious and crept along through the underbrush until he came to a clearing where he saw a dried human skin fastened by a cord to a tall pole. It swung around in the wind and watched the clearing. He was very crafty and knew that he could not approach the Hadjoqda (dried skin) without being seen and reported to its masters. Looking about he saw a mole and made a bargain with it to borrow its coat. Shrinking himself by magic he entered the mole skin and then burrowed underground until he was directly under the skin, when he broke a little root into beads and stained them with berry juice. He called to the skin and offered to give it wampum if it would talk for a while... He learned that the master sorcerer was Deadoehdjadse', and that the seven sisters cooked human flesh for him, grinding it in a corn mortar with white corn meal... Then he learned that the lives of the sorcerer and his sister were secure, for they could not be killed, their hearts being concealed under the wing of a loon that swam in a pool under a bed in the lodge.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 202-203; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he used magic to make himself appear exactly like Deadoehdjadse', and strode boldly into the clearing, chewing a strawberry and spitting the juice. This gave him great power. He drew near the lodge and called for food, but one sister was suspicious and offered him corn, then meat, then fish, but Turkey refused them all and roared that he was Ongwe I'as and wanted his accustomed dinner. This they put before him and he ate it all, satisfying the women that he was indeed their brother. Suddenly Skin Man began to call and the women all ran out of the lodge, for Skin Man was crying that the deer were in the strawberries. When the sisters were out of sight, Turkey noticed a small dog watching one of the beds. He threw a piece of meat to the dog and then lifted up the bed. Beneath was a pool of water and a loon swimming about. 'Give me the hearts,' commanded Turkey... This time the loon lifted its right wing and beneath were the eight hearts. Turkey grabbed them and ran out crying, 'I am Turkey, and I've got your hearts.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 203; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sisters saw Turkey with the hearts they began to chase him with the clubs which they used on the deer, but as each assailant approached Turkey squeezed her heart, causing her to faint... By this time the women were at the flat rock where their brother killed his victims. Turkey now threw their hearts one by one on the stone and each cracked open like a flint stone. 'Turkey has your heart, Turkey has your heart,' sang the Skin Man in derision. The monster sorcerer then rushed into the clearing where he saw Turkey dancing about the flat stone. He rushed upon him, but Turkey threw the heart upon the rock and broke both heart and rock. Then he patted Skin Man all over the body and restored him to his normal form. To his surprise he found him to be his own brother, who had been held by sorcery to obey the commands of the wizard and his sisters. Together they gathered many bones that were strewn about the flat rock. When all were piled up Turkey kicked over a pig-nut tree and called out, 'Disjointed bones, arise before this tree falls upon you!' The tree fell and before it hit the ground a great host of people arose and all were quarreling, for all had portions of the others' bodies. Turkey pacified them... and there they built a new village, and there they live to this day.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 203-204; not verbatim.

title.en: Corn Rains into Empty Barrels: The Bride from the Far South
title.zh: 玉米如雨入空桶：南國來的新娘

region.en: The hilltop of bark-eaters, and the far south land of corn
region.zh: 食樹皮者的山丘與南方的玉米之鄉

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 24, 'Corn Rains into Empty Barrels' (1923)

summary.en: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth: nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill and lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while,' while his brother tortured him with sharp stones. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path; he listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running - but nobody believed him. One morning while he sat in the doorway with his head down on his knees a young woman stood before him, smiled and handed him a basket of bread: 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man. My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces' - and soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels; the barrels were full of shelled corn, and everybody ate and all were satisfied. But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game; the young wife's food was rejected, and speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people she returned to her home - the barrels scraped bare overnight. The husband found her on a high mound covered with corn plants, her body burned and scarred where the thrown corn had struck her; and after living in the south several months the couple returned to find the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again, and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away, for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
summary.zh: 大地上曾經顆粒無存：幾乎人人餓死，倖存者聚於高丘以煮樹皮為生。有個青年總是念叨「過一陣就會好起來」，他的弟弟卻用利石折磨他。他聽見乾淨小徑上的腳步聲，守了一個月才聽見奔跑之聲——卻無人信他。一日清晨，一位少女立在他門前，微笑著遞上一籃麵包：「我母親派我來此地找一個青年，要我嫁他……我自遙遠的南方來，那裡食物充足。」她命眾人打開玉米桶的桶蓋、進屋矇住面孔——頃刻間桶中傳來玉米落下的沙沙聲，桶桶皆滿，人人吃飽。但小叔把食物丟進火裡說要吃獵物；新娘的食物遭拒，便代表全族的嫌棄回娘家去了——當夜玉米桶被刮得精光。丈夫在長滿玉米株的高丘上尋見她，她的身子被丟棄的玉米灼燒得傷痕累累；南國數月之後夫妻重返，族人又在挨餓。新娘再命他們開桶矇面，玉米如雨般落滿桶中。她告誡眾人：玉米萬不可糟蹋拋棄——它是糧食，糟蹋它便會歉收絕產。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. A food-taboo charter: wasted corn = the corn maiden's burns.

passages.text: At one time there was nothing to eat on all the earth. Nearly all the people had starved to death, and a few that remained gathered together on a high hill. They lived on boiled bark. There was a certain young man who kept saying all the time, 'It will be better after a while.' Nobody believed him because things were getting worse each day. His brother used to torture him with sharp stones and say harsh things to him. The young man, however, kept thinking that something would happen soon. After a while he heard footsteps, as if on a clean path. He listened for the span of a moon and then heard them running. He told the people but nobody believed him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 205; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One morning while he sat in the doorway of his lodge with his head down on his knees, a young woman stood before him. He heard her breathe and looked up. She smiled and handed him a basket of bread. 'My mother sent me to this lodge to find a young man,' she said. 'My mother wants me to marry him... I have come from the far south. There is plenty of food there.' So the young man ate the bread and was married to the young woman from the south. Then the young wife said, 'My mother sent me to bring food to you. Let everybody take off the tops of their corn barrels and then enter the lodge and cover their faces.' The sun had now come up and it was hot. The people did not like their faces covered, but soon they heard a sound like corn falling into their barrels. After a time the noise ceased and the young wife said, 'It is finished now.' Out into the shed went the people of the lodge and found the barrels full of shelled corn. Everybody ate and all were satisfied.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 205-206; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: But the younger brother threw his food into the fire and said he wanted game... When the husband returned he found his wife crying and when he asked her what was troubling her she said, 'Your younger brother has spoiled everything. He has rejected my food (speaking thereby the dissatisfaction of all the people). I shall now return to my home.'... During the following night there was a sound of scraping in the corn barrels and in the morning when the women went for their corn it was all gone, and with it the bride had vanished... He came to a region of great corn fields and after a while saw a high mound covered with corn plants. On this mound he found his wife and her mother.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: His wife showed him her body and it was burned and scarred. 'This is what your brother did to me,' she said, 'when he threw the corn into the fire. He would have killed me had I remained.' After living in the south for several months the couple returned and found the people again starving. The young wife ordered them to open their corn barrels and hide their faces once again. They did so and shelled corn fell like rain into the barrels filling them to the top. Then the young wife told the people that corn must never be wasted or thrown away for it is food and if destroyed will cause the crops to be poor and the corn to cease to yield.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 206-207; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker: Powers Granted Twice
title.zh: 特溫特瓜瓦與搗蛋鬼：只賜兩次的法力

region.en: Lazy man's mossy rock by the river, and the hidden bark house of S'hodie'onskon'
region.zh: 河畔懶人的青苔岩與搗蛋鬼的隱形木屋

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. VI tale 25, 'Twentgowa and the Mischief Maker' (1923)

summary.en: Twentgowa the lazy man dreams on a mossy rock by the river of killing big game if he only had a chance, until a friend appears: 'I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.' In the bark house that only appears from his bed the friend conjures the loathly mess into steaming pudding - 'Djiskwengo' - and throws the pot of food right through the wall of Twentgowa's abdomen. But the power fails at home - all that is produced is a terrible mess that drives his family out of the house - for the friend is none other than S'hodie'onskon', the mischief maker. Each gift is granted only twice: the pumpkin from the head of the war club - Twentgowa's third try whacks his own big toe and he faints; the shins whittled to bone knives to strike the fish - his second home attempt bleeds him into a faint until the friend heals the wounds with salivary fluid; the elm-bark cords and fish-bladder nose for hunting ducks underwater - on his third try the ducks he has tied draw him up into the air over the forest and drop him into an enormous hollow stub, where his drumming and song 'Djii-ha-ha' make the wood-gathering damsels dance until an axe reveals only a man with his clothes torn off. The wife gives him a terrible scolding, and the friend says: 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
summary.zh: 懶漢特溫特瓜瓦總在河畔青苔岩上空想著「若有机會必獵大獸」，直到一位朋友現身：「我家好吃好喝，梁上掛滿獵物。」只在他躺臥處才顯形的木屋裡，朋友一聲「迪斯克文戈」便把腥臭的糊漿化為香噴噴的熱布丁，還把食盆連食物隔牆送入他的腹中。可回到家法力盡失——只變出一團惡臭，把妻兒都熏出屋去——原來這位朋友正是搗蛋鬼肖迪恩斯康。每次法力只賜兩次：戰棒頭裡滾出南瓜——他第三次揮槌砸中自己的大腳趾，昏死過去；把小腿削成骨刀插水刺魚——第二次自家試法血流如注，昏倒溪邊，虧得朋友以唾液療傷；以榆皮繩與魚鰾鼻潛水獵鴨——第三次嘗試時鴨群振翅把他拖上天空、拋進巨大空樹樁，他的鼓聲與歌聲「吉—哈—哈」引得拾柴的姑娘們翩翩起舞，直到斧聲揭穿——樹洞裡不過是個衣衫被刮光的漢子。妻子把他痛罵一頓；朋友也言明：「特溫特瓜瓦不得再往河畔的青苔岩去，也不許再來我家。從今往後，他得像別的男人一樣打獵。」

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Cornplanter informant, 1905, Parker 1923); public domain.

passages.text: There was once a very lazy man named Twentgowa. He had a wife and several children. Twentgowa was always giving excuses to his wife as to why he did not hunt game more often like other men. Twentgowa often went into the deep woods and had a mossy rock near a river where he would lie and dream of the things he would like to do and how he would kill big game animals if he only had a chance... One evening a man came to the lodge where Twentgowa lived. He stood in the doorway and said: 'I am your friend. I have visited you before but this is the first time you have seen me. I have known your name for a long time. Now you must come often and see me. I have good things in my place of abode and there is plenty to eat and much game hanging on my rafters.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, p. 208; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When he had lain there a short time he looked up and saw a large bark house, with very fine poles as supports and over the door a head of some animal he could not identify... 'Come in,' said his friend, 'This is where I live... Now it is time to eat. Be seated here on a mat and let us eat together.' Thereupon the friend went to an upper shelf and took down a bowl into which he placed a loathly mess of substance that had the odor of a fish a long time dead. 'Djiskwengo,' exclaimed the friend, and the bowl filled up with steaming pudding of most enticing odor. So the two friends ate the food and relished it greatly... 'My friend, there is no need of that,' said the householder. 'I will give you power to do as I have done.' So Twentgowa stood at the back of the lodge and his friend threw the pot of food into him right through the wall of his abdomen. It vanished through magic and power was within Twentgowa.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 209-210; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: He kept thinking of his newly acquired power and thought it might be well to test it. So he sat down on a log and used his magical word, 'Odjiskwagoh.' As he did this a great pile of steaming pumpkin pudding formed on the ground... He placed in it the loathly substance like unto a dead fish and then conjured it until it overflowed... His wife was very angry and would not touch the food but scolded him, for instead of real food all that was produced was a terrible mess that drove her and the children out of the house... 'Do not go to the lodge of that man any longer. He is none other than S'hodie'onskon', whom we know as a mischief maker. He will make your mind abnormal and what is bad he will make you think is good.' The second gift: pumpkins from the head of the war club - 'I will give you power to so produce twice... Stand, swing your war club until it comes whack against the head of my club' - and at home Twentgowa lifted up his foot upon the bench and whacked his big toe: it was a terrible and resounding whack, but no pumpkin rolled forth; Twentgowa fell off the bench like a dead man.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 210-212; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So saying he went out and strode down to the creek where he removed his leggings. He took out his knife and passed it through his lips, moistening it. Then he began to whittle the meat off his shins so that the bone stood out sharp like a long knife. 'Now, my friend,' said he, 'I will wade swiftly through the water and strike the fishes before they can move to one side.'... Coming ashore he put down his basket and then began to moisten his shins with salivary fluid. They quickly were restored and did not bleed at any time... At length, despairing of causing him harm in this manner... Twentgowa tried his new power and caught many fish which he left with his friend... At home As he cut the flesh blood flowed out and he was in great pain... She dragged him to the lodge and then called upon her dog to go and fetch S'hondie'onskon', the magical friend, to come and heal the husband... Then said the friend, 'I gave you power twice, but further than that I did not give you. You have cheated and wasted your power.' The last gift was duck-hunting under water with elm bark cords and a fish's air-bladder touched to his nose: at home, into the lake he went for he saw upon its surface a great flock of ducks swimming closely together... Upward flew the ducks with such impetus that Twentgowa was drawn up into the air and over the forest. When the ducks had flown a short way the string which he was holding broke and down he fell and into the top of an enormous hollow stub... Twentgowa then sang 'Djii-ha-ha, djii-ha-ha!' many times, and the damsel danced... He took an axe and chopped down the tree... and there inside was a man with his clothes torn off. The wife scolded him for making the damsels dance... Then the friend came out of the bushes where he was hiding and he said, 'Twentgowa must not go to the woods any more to the spot where he has been accustomed to recline. He may not come to my house any more. Henceforth he must hunt like other men.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1923, pp. 213-216; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
